entities.name: Henry IV of England
entities.label: Person
entities.summary:
Henry IV (born Henry Bolingbroke in April 1367), Duke of Lancaster, seized the English throne in 1399, deposing his cousin Richard II, an act that fundamentally reshaped the English monarchy and set a precedent for dynastic instability that culminated in the Wars of the Roses. His reign, lasting until his death on March 20, 1413, marked the ascendancy of the House of Lancaster, inheriting the crowns of England and France (the latter titularly) and the lordship of Ireland, while also holding the Duchy of Aquitaine. His usurpation, driven by political grievances and Richard II's perceived tyranny, established a new constitutional dynamic where parliamentary consent gained increased, albeit contested, importance in validating monarchical power.

Henry's reign was characterized by continuous challenges to his legitimacy and authority, both at home and abroad. He faced numerous rebellions, most notably the Welsh uprising led by Owain Glyndŵr (1400-1415), and the Percy family rebellion culminating in the Battle of Shrewsbury in 1403, where Henry personally fought and defeated Harry Hotspur. To secure his precarious position, Henry relied heavily on Parliament, granting it unprecedented powers over taxation and legislation, which laid groundwork for future constitutional developments. He also faced ongoing border conflicts with Scotland and piracy in the English Channel, requiring significant military expenditure and diplomatic maneuvering.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: Henry IV's usurpation of the English throne fundamentally altered the course of English dynastic politics, directly contributing to the later Wars of the Roses. His reign also saw a significant increase in the power and influence of the English Parliament, setting precedents for future constitutional development.
